card.hook: You'll hear the cathedral before you've decided where to point your phone. People stop mid-stride, tip their heads back and say "wow". Its two spires reach 157 m, so it's the tallest twin-spired church in the world.
card.stand_here: Stand at Kardinal-Höffner-Platz, about 90 m west of the cathedral, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade in. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the spires and carved stone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, line both towers up with the vertical lines, and hold your phone upright and level so they don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. After dark, try night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the padlock-covered railings on the southern pedestrian walkway of the Hohenzollern Bridge. Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the cathedral towers behind you and the colourful padlocks all around.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far end of Roncalliplatz, on the cathedral's south side, facing north toward the main façade, while you stand in front of them with the whole façade behind you (zoom 0.5x fits the full front).
card.rules_and_safety: On Burgmauer Street, watch out for cars and bikes. The cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site before going inside or up the tower.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead straight in one shot, then add a row of passers-by at the bottom to show how tiny we all are.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1248 and stopped around 1560. It picked up again in the 1800s and was finished to its original medieval plan in 1880. It became a World Heritage Site in 1996 and is Germany's most visited landmark, so expect company. It was built to house the Shrine of the Three Kings, a medieval goldsmith's masterpiece.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Kardinal-Höffner-Platz, about 90 m west of the cathedral, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.

card.hook: Most people hurry through Cologne Central Station with their eyes on the departure board. Look up for a second: a big, busy station sits right beside a giant stone cathedral, and that clash is the whole photo.
card.stand_here: Head to Chargesheimerplatz, about 100 m south-west of the station, to the phone icon on the map. Face north-east and the station fills much of your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole frontage. If it won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for signs, roof shapes or people at the entrances.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the station up with them, then keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you a clear, even view of the whole frontage. Around dusk the lit windows and signs add atmosphere, and night mode can handle the lower light. Quieter hours mean fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in behind you. Keep the station over your shoulder and hold the phone a little further out than feels natural.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy public transport building. If you step inside, keep your phone steady and don't block walkways, and check the official site before you go, since photography rules can change.
card.challenge: Wait for a good mix of passers-by crossing your foreground, then snap the one shot where it looks like everyone is rushing except you.
card.good_to_know: The first station here opened on 5 December 1859, together with the first Rhine bridge beside the cathedral. What you see today is mostly post-war, and the new hall with its shell-shaped roof was inaugurated on 23 September 1957. About 320,000 travellers pass through on an average day, which makes it the fifth busiest station in Germany.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Chargesheimerplatz, about 100 m south-west of the station, to the phone icon on the map. Face north-east and the station fills much of your view.

card.hook: There's a glass-and-steel ship moored on the Rhine, and it's packed with chocolate. The best photo of it is from across the water, not from the busy front door.
card.stand_here: Cross to Deutzer Hafen on the Deutz (right) bank of the Rhine and face the museum across the river. Move along the bank until the cathedral shows up beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to see the whole scene. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the distant museum closer. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the building tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the museum, then drag the brighter/darker slider down a touch so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the water. Pick a day when the sky is clear enough to show the cathedral too.
card.selfie_here: Walk down the Deutz bank, away from the cathedral, and turn your back to the water so the museum sits behind you. The museum's own photo guide says you can get the cathedral and the Chocolate Museum in the background from this side. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the riverside promenade in front of the museum, ask a passer-by to shoot with the Rhine in the foreground so the whole ship-shaped building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the museum are fine for personal, non-commercial use, but flash isn't allowed. The museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site if you want to go in.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap between passing boats, then get the river along the bottom of your shot with the museum and cathedral side by side.
card.good_to_know: Hans Imhoff opened the museum on 31 October 1993. The building was designed with post-modern ship motifs, which is why it looks like a vessel at the water's edge. With around 650,000 visitors a year, it's the most visited museum in Cologne.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross to Deutzer Hafen on the Deutz (right) bank of the Rhine and face the museum across the river. Move along the bank until the cathedral shows up beside it.

card.hook: You step through the door and your head tips back before you've even decided to look up. That's Cologne Cathedral inside: tall, narrow and a bit hard to take in at first.
card.stand_here: Start near Papstterrasse, about 45 m west of the subject (that's the phone icon on the map), and face east. Once you're inside, keep facing east and look along the main space from the middle, out of the aisles.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full height and both side walls in one shot. Switch to zoom 1x for a single arch or a quiet corner, then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for windows and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tall columns up with the vertical lines so the walls stand straight, then tap a plain part of the wall and drag to darker so the bright windows keep their colour.
card.best_time: Daytime is usually best because the windows are at their brightest. Early in the day or late in the afternoon is often quieter, but check the official site for visiting times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the Gerhard Richter window or the Shrine of the Three Kings, both named by the cathedral's own guide as top indoor photo spots. Use the front camera, hold it a little higher than usual, and let the window or shrine sit behind your shoulder. Keep the flash off.
card.ask_someone: For a full-building shot with you in it, step outside to Roncalliplatz on the south side, ask a passer-by to stand at the far end of the square facing north toward the main facade, and stand in front of the cathedral yourself.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your voice low, don't use flash, and don't block the aisles. Dress respectfully, and check the official site for entry, photography and bag rules, as they can change.
card.challenge: Find a patch of coloured window light on a wall or pillar and get a close-up of it, then see if a friend can guess which window it came from.
card.good_to_know: This is a working place of worship and it's usually busy, so be patient and wait for a gap in the crowd. The large windows fill the tall, narrow space with coloured light. Some parts may be ticketed, so check before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Papstterrasse, about 45 m west of the subject (that's the phone icon on the map), and face east. Once you're inside, keep facing east and look along the main space from the middle, out of the aisles.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: the building you're aiming at is a modern art museum and a concert hall sharing one roof. That makes it a big, busy subject, so you'll want to step back.
card.stand_here: Stand on Heinrich-Böll-Platz, about 35 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the building. If it won't all fit, tap 0.5x. Save 2x or more for a doorway or a window.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the building's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Morning is likely your best bet, because the sun should be behind you and light up the side you can see. On a bright day, skip the midday glare.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little higher so the building fits over your shoulder. Turn so the museum is behind you, then check the edges aren't leaning before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Private, non-commercial photos are allowed inside the museum, but flash and selfie sticks are not. Photography isn't permitted in temporary exhibitions, and Heinrich-Böll-Platz can't be walked on during concerts.
card.challenge: Get a wide shot first, then a close-up of an entrance or a facade detail, and catch a few passers-by in the wide one to show how big the place is.
card.good_to_know: Museum Ludwig opened in 1986 and was designed by Peter Busmann and Godfrid Haberer, close to Cologne Cathedral. The Kölner Philharmonie is in the same building, and Heinrich-Böll-Platz, designed by Dani Karavan, sits above the concert hall. Inside, there are around 900 Picasso works, the third largest Picasso collection in the world after Barcelona and Paris.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Heinrich-Böll-Platz, about 35 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.

The only named spot (the 'Brushstrokes' sculpture) comes from one Trip.com page whose wording looks generic; I could not confirm the sculpture exists, so check it on a map before sending visitors there. A second selfie spot was not found: the rooftop terrace and café views are inside the museum and face the bridge and cathedral, not the building. The ask-someone spot is inferred from a Wikimedia photo's camera position on the bridge; it is not a stated photo spot for the whole museum, and the museum sits at the edge of that frame, so a full-building shot from there is doubtful. The museum's no-flash, no-tripod, no-selfie-stick rules come from its own site, so they are the firmest part of this answer.

card.hook: Picture a 61-metre tower peeking over a row of colourful gabled houses, with a statue-topped fountain right in front of you. That's the Alter Markt postcard, and it's easier to get than it looks.
card.stand_here: Stand beside the Jan von Werth fountain, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face south toward the Rathaus, so the City Hall tower rises over the gabled houses.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view of the houses, tower and fountain. Tap 0.5x if the crowd or the Christmas stalls make it hard to fit everything in, or 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower over the rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the fountain on the right and the tower near the centre line, and keep your phone level so the houses don't lean.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, so you get a cleaner view of the fountain and houses. Low sun is lovely on the painted plaster of the Gaffel Haus gable, and in Christmas market season the evening is the time for the lights (but expect crowds).
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the Jan von Werth fountain in the middle of the square, with the Rathaus side behind you. Use the front camera, and if yours has a 0.5x button, tap it to squeeze in more of the old-town buildings over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Alter Markt is an open public square, but for events like the Christmas market or Carnival, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the fountain on the right, the tower dead centre and every house standing up straight? Bonus points if nobody's head is in the way.
card.good_to_know: The City Hall tower is 61 metres tall. The stepped gable of the Gaffel Haus is a great second subject on the same square, and the Fischmarkt with its colourful houses is right next door. When Carnival opens at 11:11, big crowds gather around the fountain, so hold your phone a little higher or just let the people be part of the fun.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand beside the Jan von Werth fountain, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face south toward the Rathaus, so the City Hall tower rises over the gabled houses.

card.hook: Pastel gabled houses in a neat row, and right behind them a huge stone tower, like a very old giant peeking over the neighbours' fence. That's Great St. Martin from Fischmarkt, and it's the shot everyone comes for.
card.stand_here: Stand on Fischmarkt, the cobbled square in front of the church, with the Rhine behind you. Face west toward the church, so the tower and its eastern end rise above the gabled houses.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the tower, the church's eastern end and the houses in one go. If the square is busy or you want more houses, drop to 0.5x. For a tighter shot of the tower top, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, then tap the tower and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: One guide says late afternoon gives warm light on the tower, and another suggests early morning for the eastern light. Either way, check the light on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try Fischmarkt, in front of the row of brightly painted houses, with the church tower rising behind them. Blogs call it the classic Old Town backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the church over your shoulder. The exact direction isn't given, so test whether the church or the river ends up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the edge of Fischmarkt facing the church's west front, while you stand in front of the painted houses with the tower rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship with reduced opening hours, so check the official site before you go if you want to step inside.
card.challenge: Can you get the tower on a gridline, the cobbles at your feet, and no stranger's head sticking out of a gable?
card.good_to_know: The church's foundations date from around 960 AD and sit on the remains of a Roman chapel. The buildings you see today went up between 1150 and 1250, and the eastern end has an unusual clover-leaf plan of three apses. A storm in 1434 knocked down three of the four tower gables, and one landed on a nearby fish market.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Fischmarkt, the cobbled square in front of the church, with the Rhine behind you. Face west toward the church, so the tower and its eastern end rise above the gabled houses.

card.hook: Picture a train sliding into a long tunnel of iron arches while the Rhine glints below. That's the Hohenzollern Bridge, and with more than 1,200 trains a day you rarely wait long for it.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Kurt-Rossa-Platz, about 230 m west of the subject, and face east. The bridge stretches out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in as much of the span as you can, then switch to 1x for a tidier crop. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and a passing train.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the ironwork looks dark and crisp.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light on the ironwork. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep steady.
card.selfie_here: Walk out to the middle of the bridge's north footpath, turn your back to the love-lock railing and use the front camera so the cathedral sits behind you. Guides disagree on which side holds the locks, so check which walkway has them when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the upper terrace of the Rheinboulevard in Deutz, facing the bridge and cathedral, while you stand in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos from the public footpaths on the bridge are fine, and you don't need a platform ticket. Stay on the footpath, because the tracks are working railway land and off limits. Check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.
card.challenge: Line up the arches on your lower third and wait for a train to roll in, then grab a burst or a Live Photo and pick your favourite moment.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was built between 1907 and 1911 and opened by Kaiser Wilhelm II on 22 May 1911. It's 409 metres long, was blown up in 1945, and the rebuilt version was finished in 1959. Look for the statues of Prussian kings and emperors by the ramps, and the love padlocks, which were estimated at around 500,000 in June 2015.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near Kurt-Rossa-Platz, about 230 m west of the subject, and face east. The bridge stretches out in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: Sources describe the mid-bridge railing as the densest and most varied lock display, and a visitor posing at the lock wall with the cathedral blurred behind is an example of this exact shot.

card.hook: A low, modern building sits at the foot of a giant cathedral, and the cathedral is clearly the show-off. That contrast is the whole fun of this shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Roncalliplatz, in front of the museum's facade. The museum is to the north-east of you, with the cathedral rising behind it, so face that way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the low museum frontage and the cathedral in together. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look, or try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to home in on the cathedral towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level so the cathedral doesn't lean, and tap the cathedral, then slide it a bit darker if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go earlier or later in the day, when the softer light flatters the cathedral stonework. Harsh midday sun is the one to avoid.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little higher than your face. Turn around so the big landmark sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the open area south of the Cathedral (the Domplatte) and ask a passer-by to frame you with the whole museum building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The main building is closed for renovation, so the front may be partly hidden by works.
card.challenge: Get the museum as a low band across the bottom and the cathedral filling the space above, with the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1974 on the site of a 3rd-century Roman villa, found in 1941. The Dionysus mosaic, from around A.D. 220/230, still lies where the Romans laid it. For now the collection is shown at the Belgian House, Cäcilienstraße 46, which is a different building and not part of this photo spot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Roncalliplatz, in front of the museum's facade. The museum is to the north-east of you, with the cathedral rising behind it, so face that way.

ask_someone_spot.name: Open area south of Cologne Cathedral (Domplatte)
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on the open area to the south of the Cathedral, where the museum's own history page says the building is seen from. Ask the passer-by to frame you with the museum's facade behind the whole building. The museum is currently closed for renovation, so this shows the closed building, not an open museum.

The ask-someone spot is the open area south of the Cathedral, named on the museum's own History page as the place from which the building is seen; the source does not describe it as a photo spot, so check it on the map before use. A German photo guide (germanywander.com) suggests shooting the Cathedral towers from 'the corner near the Roman-Germanic Museum' on Roncalliplatz, but that describes a photo of the Cathedral, not of a visitor with the museum behind, so I left it out. No page I found gives selfie-stick or tripod rules or a safety point for this site.

card.hook: Cologne's town hall looks like it was assembled by committee over 900 years, and honestly, that's its charm. Tilt your head back at the 61-metre tower and you'll spot stone figures everywhere.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rathausplatz, the open square in front of the City Hall, and face the building so the Gothic tower and the Renaissance loggia sit side by side in your frame. Keep a little of the square at the bottom of the shot to show how big it all is.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower, loggia and square into one picture. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the stone figures and the clock.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold your phone upright and level, and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people. If you want the clock figure, get there a few minutes before the hour.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Rathausplatz with the Gothic tower and loggia behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit lower so the landmark fits over your shoulder. Alter Markt is another option, as reviewers say it gives the best view of the tower.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the fountain on Alter Markt facing south toward the City Hall, while you stand in front of the Rathaus with it behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The space between the historic building and the Spanischer Bau is closed on wedding days, so check the official site before you go, especially if you want to reach the main entrance. One report says construction has blocked some views at the back, so it's worth a quick look on site.
card.challenge: Find a loggia arch and frame it so the tower peeks out above it, then see if a friend can spot it in your photo.
card.good_to_know: This is Germany's oldest town hall, with a documented history of some 900 years. The Gothic council tower was finished in the 1410s, and the Renaissance loggia was built between 1569 and 1573. Much of the complex was destroyed in the war and rebuilt, and the tower's bells play a carillon four times a day.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Rathausplatz, the open square in front of the City Hall, and face the building so the Gothic tower and the Renaissance loggia sit side by side in your frame. Keep a little of the square at the bottom of the shot to show how big it all is.

selfie_spots.why: Reviewers say the Alter Markt gives the best view of the tower, so it is the most likely place to get the landmark behind you.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: the name 4711 started as a plain house number, handed out when the French numbered Cologne's buildings in 1794. That house is long gone, but the number stuck, and now it's the most photogenic street front on Glockengasse.
card.stand_here: Cross to the opposite side of Glockengasse and face the 4711 House at number 4, with the neo-Gothic front and the carillon in view. The street is narrow, so you'll need to back up against the shops opposite.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole façade in, then try 1x for a less stretched look. For the carillon (the Glockenspiel), zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so the house stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: The façade is said to look especially good when it's lit up at Christmas, so try night mode then and hold the phone steady against a wall. At other times, daylight shows off the stonework and the lettering nicely.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the neo-Gothic façade on Glockengasse with the building behind you, front camera tilted up a little so the 4711 lettering is over your shoulder. Inside the ground-floor store, the lit 4711 sign makes a good backdrop too, with the wall tapestry and spiral staircase nearby.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the corner where Glockengasse meets Schwertergasse and shoot toward the façade, while you pose on the pavement in front of the house.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are generally fine inside the main store area, but be mindful of other guests and staff. The house is also a shop and museum, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole building and the full 4711 name in one frame with straight sides, then sneak in a second shot of just the carillon.
card.good_to_know: The 4711 House is the original shop of the famous Eau de Cologne brand, and the scent has been made in Cologne since at least 1799. It's still a working shop and museum, so decide whether you want a quick street photo or a visit inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross to the opposite side of Glockengasse and face the 4711 House at number 4, with the neo-Gothic front and the carillon in view. The street is narrow, so you'll need to back up against the shops opposite.

card.hook: Picture a Romanesque church tower standing in its own open square, with trees around it like a soft frame. That's St. Ursula's, and it's a rare Cologne church you can actually step back from.
card.stand_here: Stand in Ursulaplatz, in the middle of the square, and face the church front and tower. Back up until the west front and bell tower both fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole west front and tower. If the tower won't fit, tap 0.5x, which also lets in more trees and square. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower, the doorway and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the tower, and keep your phone upright so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight, when the front is lit, shows the stonework best. Afternoon to early evening will likely give warmer light on the west front, and going early should mean fewer people on the square.
card.selfie_here: Try Ursulaplatz beside the Schreckenskammer tavern (Ursulaplatz 11), which sits right next to the church. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the basilica over your shoulder. One reviewer found the church striking from here at night against a dark sky, but check the spot on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography in the Golden Chamber may be restricted, so look for signs or ask first. Flash inside the church is usually discouraged, and the church's official site is the place to check before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly straight on a grid line with a tree peeking into the corner of the frame. Bonus points if you're grinning in front of it.
card.good_to_know: St. Ursula's is one of Cologne's twelve Romanesque churches. The nave and main tower are Romanesque, while the choir was rebuilt in Gothic style. It became a Minor Basilica on 25 June 1920 and sits on the site of an ancient Roman cemetery. Inside, the Golden Chamber has walls covered in bones arranged in patterns and letters, found in 1106 in a mass grave.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Ursulaplatz, in the middle of the square, and face the church front and tower. Back up until the west front and bell tower both fit in one frame.

card.hook: Three chunky buildings stand beside the Rhine, each shaped like the harbour cranes that used to work here. They're the Kranhaus blocks, and they look great from a bridge.
card.stand_here: Go onto the footpath of Severinsbrücke and stop where you can look south along the harbour. Face south toward the Rheinauhafen, and all three crane houses sit in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit all three buildings in one frame. Try 0.5x to bring in more of the bridge's steel arch, or 2x if your phone has it for a tighter shot of those angled shapes.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the buildings, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go for blue hour, just after sunset, when the dusk colours suit the bridge view. If you use night mode, stand steady and wait for any shaking to stop before you tap.
card.selfie_here: Head to the 'Alaaf' lettering on Harry-Blum-Platz in the Rheinauhafen. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the cathedral and the crane houses over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you, stand on the pedestrian walkway of the Deutzer Brücke, ask a passer-by to face south toward the Rheinauhafen, and stand in front of them so all three Kranhäuser are behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The 'Alaaf' sign is a Carnival-season installation, so it may not be there at other times. Check before you go. Also check the official site for any closures or works, as we haven't confirmed current ones.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line one vertical line up with the edge of the middle building, Kranhaus1, so it stands up straight. It's the award winner, so it deserves the neat framing.
card.good_to_know: The Rheinauhafen is a former commercial harbour, developed in the 1880s. It's now a district of offices, cultural venues, hotels and homes, with a marina in the old harbour basin. Regeneration began in 2002. From south to north the crane houses are KranhausPLUS, Kranhaus1 and Pandion Vista, and Kranhaus1 won an international award in 2009.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go onto the footpath of Severinsbrücke and stop where you can look south along the harbour. Face south toward the Rheinauhafen, and all three crane houses sit in front of you.

card.hook: There's a giant stone head of a saint sitting in front of a church, and it's looking at you. Nobody needs to explain why that's worth a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in front of St. Gereon's Basilica on the park side, near Gereonskloster. Face the church so the towers and rounded apse rise behind the sculpted head of St. Gereon, if you can find it. Check on the day exactly where it stands.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the church, or for the head and church together. If the towers get cut off, tap 0.5x. For a tighter shot of the towers and apse, try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church, then slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't turn white, and turn on the gridlines to line up a church wall with a vertical line.
card.best_time: Go on a bright, softly overcast day. The even light is kind to the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie beside the large stone head of St. Gereon in the grounds in front of the church, which reviewers call very photogenic and easy to find from Gereonskloster. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if it's available, and try to get the church over your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed the church shows up behind the head, so check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the corner of Gereonskloster and Gereonshof, where the view back toward the church tower shows off the building's bulk, and ask for a shot with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the basilica is generally allowed, but without flash. Opening arrangements for the interior aren't given here, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Put the stone head in the lower part of your frame, let the towers rise behind it, and see if you can make it look like the saint is photobombing his own church.
card.good_to_know: The oldest part is an oval Roman building from the second half of the 4th century, and a church here is first mentioned in 612. The east end, with its two square towers and rounded apse, was added in the 12th century. In the 13th century the old core was topped with a decagonal dome, the largest built in the West between Hagia Sophia and the cathedral in Florence.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in front of St. Gereon's Basilica on the park side, near Gereonskloster. Face the church so the towers and rounded apse rise behind the sculpted head of St. Gereon, if you can find it. Check on the day exactly where it stands.

card.hook: Picture a giant concrete staircase leading down to the Rhine, with Cologne Cathedral and the Hohenzollern Bridge lined up across the water like they're waiting for you. That's the Deutz side, and it's the classic postcard view with a seat included.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Rheinboulevard, on the upper terrace or the wide concrete steps on the Deutz (east) bank of the Rhine. Face west across the river toward the Cathedral and the bridge.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the Cathedral and the bridge side by side. Go to 0.5x if you want more river and sky. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Cathedral on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and keep the river along the bottom third, so the water stays level and nothing leans.
card.best_time: Sunset into just after is the sweet spot, when the light goes golden and then blue. If you'd like it quieter, go early in the morning. After dark, use night mode and hold your phone as still as you can.
card.selfie_here: Head to the small bay at the Deutz end of the Hohenzollern Bridge, next to the equestrian statue. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and put the Cathedral and the bridge over your shoulder. It works solo or with one friend.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the upper terrace while you sit on the lower concrete steps, so the Cathedral and the bridge fill the frame behind you. Ask them to try 0.5x or 1x so they catch it all.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public terrace and set of steps by the river. Check the official site before you go in case of any closures.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice: once standing on the upper terrace, once sitting low on the steps. Which one gives you more river?
card.good_to_know: The Rheinboulevard has an upper terrace and wide concrete steps that face west across the water. The steps are a ready-made viewing platform, so you can pick your height and take your time. For other angles, try the Deutzer Brücke for a skyline view or Rheinpark for a wider sweep across open water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Rheinboulevard, on the upper terrace or the wide concrete steps on the Deutz (east) bank of the Rhine. Face west across the river toward the Cathedral and the bridge.

Sources disagree on which Kaiser (Wilhelm I or II) the Deutz-end bridge statue depicts, so I used a neutral description. The selfie-spot sources focus on the Cathedral view rather than selfies, and the styleREBELLES page is about 5 years old.

card.hook: There's a Cologne skyscraper with the Cathedral printed on its skin, and whether you can see it depends on the light. Watch the glass for a minute and the picture seems to change.
card.stand_here: Stand at the lakeside stand-here point in MediaPark, by the artificial lake. From there the tower is to the east, about 1 minute on foot, so face east across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the tower and its reflection. If you walk to the foot of the tower, switch to 0.5x and tilt your phone up for the full height. Zoom 2x gets you in closer on the upper glass.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the water's edge on a lower line, then tap the tower and slide the picture a little darker so the glass keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go when the water is still, because that's when the reflection looks best. The pictures on the glass change with the light, so if you have time, check the tower at different times of day.
card.selfie_here: Try the lake edge in MediaPark with the KölnTurm behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little low so the tower rises over your shoulder. Nobody has pinned down the exact bank, so wander along the water until the tower and lake both fit.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the foot of the tower while you stand at its base, and have them tilt up so the glass climbs behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: If you want a photo in front of the lit wall inside the tower's lower-level foyer, ask at the building's entrance for permission first. It's an office building, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Can you get the tower and its reflection with not a single ripple in the water? Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: The KölnTurm is a 44-storey glass office tower, 148.5 m high, or 165.48 m with its antenna. It was built between June 1999 and November 2001 and designed by Kohl & Kohl with the Paris architect Jean Nouvel. It's the second-tallest building in Cologne, after the Cathedral.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the lakeside stand-here point in MediaPark, by the artificial lake. From there the tower is to the east, about 1 minute on foot, so face east across the water.

selfie_research.notes: Identified the landmark as the KölnTurm in Mediapark: the coordinates match its published GPS point (about 50.9481, 6.9431). 'Cologne Tower' can also refer to the Colonius, but the coordinates rule that out. None of the pages describes a selfie spot with the tower directly behind a visitor; the spots above come from photographer guides and are unverified. The Mediapark lake spot is named only in a photo-spot listing, and no page gives its exact bank. No page states selfie-stick or tripod rules for the KölnTurm, and no safety point applies to this site. The KölnTriangle pages were excluded because they are a different tower across the Rhine.

card.hook: Here's a twist: the best view of Cologne Cathedral is from a building that isn't the Cathedral. Go up the KölnTriangle and you get both spires, the Rhine and the whole skyline in one go.
card.stand_here: The phone icon sits on the KölnTriangle building itself, so you take your photos from the observation deck at the top. Face across the Rhine towards the Cathedral.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole skyline in. Use 1x for most shots, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Cathedral's spires.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the Cathedral, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer light and a warmer sky. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a ledge to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the red 'Cologne View' pillar outside the right-hand door at the Ottoplatz 1 entrance, or the Deutz end of the Hohenzollern Bridge, where the tower is on your right as you cross from the east bank. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the tower over your shoulder. Both spots are worked out from entrance and bridge descriptions, so check them when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Ottoplatz side facing the tower entrance at Ottoplatz 1, while you stand in front of the door so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The platform closes during storms. Access can change too, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Walk the whole deck and find the side where the river leads your eye straight to the twin spires.
card.good_to_know: The KölnTriangle is a 103-metre high-rise in Deutz, directly across the Rhine from Cologne Cathedral. Architect Dörte Gatermann designed it and it was finished in 2006. The public deck is on the top floor and roof, and glass reflections can be a nuisance, so hold your phone close to the glass or railing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon sits on the KölnTriangle building itself, so you take your photos from the observation deck at the top. Face across the Rhine towards the Cathedral.
